blocks.text: 9.3.1 A Binding-Constraints Report

GridCap's base plan for the small portfolio is solved: 27 of 40 projects, NPV $24,260k, every rule kept (the plan of lessons 6.4.1 and 7.1.4). The planning director now asks the question every review of an optimized plan starts with: *which of our rules actually shaped this plan?* If the answer is "the 2030 budget", finance knows where an extra dollar would matter; if it is "the alternative rule on asset A001", the asset team knows which decision to revisit. The job this course prepares for, building the optimization engine of a utility's capital planning tool (a Capital Investment Planning & Prioritization Tool, CIPT for short), lists this output by name, next to shadow prices and marginal values: the binding constraints.

This lesson builds a **binding-constraints report** for a MILP plan, in three rules. The first is the definition, read straight off the plan. The second separates "binding" from "priced", which a popular shortcut runs together. The third is the part that is new for integer models: a row with money left can still be the row that blocks every project that might be added.
GridCap is a fictional utility, generated for this course; no number in it describes a real one.

Three words first. A **row** is one constraint of the model, with the name the code gave it (`budget_2030`). Its **activity** is the value of its left-hand side at the plan: for a budget row, what the plan spends that year. Its **slack** is how far the activity is from the row's limit, measured so that a row the plan keeps has slack $`\ge 0`$:

A row **binds** at a plan when its slack is zero (in practice, within a small tolerance such as $`10^{-6}`$, because solvers work in floating point; lesson 10.1.1). This is the definition lesson 2.3.2 used for an LP, and it applies to any plan, from any model, because it needs only the plan and the row.
The Model
The rows this lesson reports on are those of the timing model of lesson 6.4.1, unchanged. Each has a name, and the report speaks in those names.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years, 2027 to 2031; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years project $`i`$ may use (its window); $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set of projects; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work, $`k = 0, 1, \dots`$ ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).

**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$. We write $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$ and $`\text{by}(i, t) = \sum_{s \in T_i,\, s \le t} x_{i,s}`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\text{by}(c, t) &\le \text{by}(p(c),\, t - L_c) && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}
`explain_model.build` writes this model and keeps every row in a dictionary by name, so a report can go from a name to the row and back.
A Row Binds When the Plan Leaves It No Slack

Slack needs nothing from the solver but the plan. MathOpt keeps each row's bounds (`lower_bound`, `upper_bound`, infinite when absent) and its nonzero terms (`terms()`, each a `LinearTerm` with a `variable` and a `coefficient`), so the definition above becomes:

One function covers all three kinds of row: a $`\le`$ row has only an upper bound, a $`\ge`$ row only a lower one, and an equality row has both, equal, so the smaller of the two rooms is $`-|a^\top x - b|`$. The `values` dictionary gives each start variable its 0 or 1 in the plan (`plan_values`), which is what the solver returned, rounded.
`slack_report.py` measures every row of the model at the base plan and counts, for each family of rules, how many rows bind:

OPTIMAL: NPV $24,260k, 27 of 40 projects funded

family  rows  binding  least slack
once      36       23            0
must       4        4            0
alt        2        2            0
after      2        2            0
budget     5        0           50

row          limit    used  slack
budget_2027   8,890   8,750    140
budget_2028   8,120   7,970    150
budget_2029   8,760   8,630    130
budget_2030   8,610   8,560     50
budget_2031   7,850   7,720    130
Read it family by family, because "binds" means something different in each.

items: **once:** 23 of the 36 rows bind, one for each funded project that is not a must-do (27 funded, less the 4 must-dos). A once row binds exactly when its project is in the plan. That says the project was chosen; it does not say the rule held anything back.
**must:** all 4 bind, always: an equality row that the plan keeps has slack 0 by definition.
**alt:** both groups have one option funded (P001 in G001, P031 in G030), so both rows bind. These do hold something back: P002 and P030 cannot join while their alternatives are in.
**after:** both precedence rows of P016 bind; P016 starts in 2030, the year its parent P015 allows.
**budget:** no budget row binds. Every year has money left, $50k to $150k.

blocks.text: So a list of zero-slack rows, on its own, says that the plan used the rules it used, and leaves out the rule everyone knows shaped the plan: the money. The next two rules explain why both happen.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A MILP Has No Prices, and Binding Means Zero Slack Even When the Price Is Zero

For an LP, lesson 2.3.3 read a second number for each row: its **shadow price** (MathOpt's `dual_values`), the change in the best objective per unit of the row's bound. Ask the MILP for one and MathOpt refuses:
MILP dual_values: ValueError: Best solution does not have an associated dual feasible solution.

The MathOpt source says why in its docstrings: dual solutions are returned only for convex problems such as LPs, so a MIP solve has none. Lesson 9.2.1 shows what goes wrong with the idea of a price on a MILP, and lessons 9.2.2 to 9.2.4 build the prices that do mean something. For this report it settles one thing: on a MILP, "binding" has to be read from slack, because there is no price to read.

The LP relaxation (every $`x_{i,t}`$ allowed between 0 and 1, lesson 3.1.1) does have prices, and it shows why the two numbers must stay separate even where both exist. `zero_price.py` solves it and sorts every row by whether it binds and whether its price is zero:

for name, row in relaxed.rows.items():
    binding = abs(slack(row, values)) <= TOL
    priced = abs(result.dual_values(row)) > TOL
    kinds[family(name), "binding" if binding else "slack", "priced" if priced else "price 0"] += 1

LP relaxation: OPTIMAL, NPV $26,587.4k

family  slack?    price?   rows
after   binding   price 0     1
after   slack     price 0     1
alt     binding   priced      2
budget  binding   priced      5
must    binding   price 0     1
must    binding   priced      3
once    binding   price 0     9
once    binding   priced     11
once    slack     price 0    16

must_P003    slack   0  price    0.0000
must_P039    slack   0  price -663.3661
budget_2031  slack   0  price    0.3158
P003: NPV 107, uses 2031 budget worth 140 x 0.3158 = 44.2

Eleven rows bind with a price of exactly zero: one precedence row, nine once rows and the must-do row of P003. Take P003. It is a must-do, so its row is an equality and binds. But at the LP's prices P003 is worth funding anyway: it brings $107k of NPV and uses $140k of 2031 budget that the LP values at $0.3158k per $1k, $44.2k in all. Remove the must-do row and the LP would still fund P003, so the row has no effect on the optimum, and its price, the effect of moving its bound, is zero. Compare P039, a must-do the LP would not choose on its own: its row binds with price $-663.37$, the NPV the plan gives up per unit of "P039 must start" (negative because raising the bound costs value; lesson 2.3.3 covers the signs).

A binding row with a zero price is the mark of a **degenerate** LP optimum (lesson 2.2.3): more rows are tight at the vertex than are needed to pin it, and some of them carry no price. Complementary slackness (lesson 2.3.2) only forbids the other combination, a row with slack and a nonzero price; every row in the table that has slack has price 0.

Some study guides define a binding row as "zero slack *and* a nonzero shadow price". This course does not, and the table shows why: under that definition must_P003 would not bind, though the plan sits exactly on it. Keep the definition (zero slack) and report the price, where one exists, in its own column. "Binds and is priced" means the rule is costing value at the margin; "binds at price 0" means the plan touches the rule without being pushed by it.
On a MILP, a Row With Slack Can Still Be the Row That Blocks

Back to the MILP plan, and to the budgets that bind nowhere. Projects are whole: a row with $50k left in 2030 cannot take any project that needs more than $50k in 2030, and in GridCap small none needs so little. So the useful question for an integer plan is not only "which rows have no slack?" but "which rows refuse the next project?".

`binding.refusals` answers it directly. For each project the plan leaves out and each year it may start in, it adds that one start to the plan as it stands and lists the rows the result breaks (negative slack):

25 single additions tried, 0 fit

row          slack  refuses
budget_2027    140   3 of 25
budget_2028    150   7 of 25
budget_2029    130   9 of 25
budget_2030     50  15 of 25
budget_2031    130   9 of 25
alt_G001         0   2 of 25
alt_G030         0   2 of 25

add P004 in 2028: breaks budget_2028 (needs 300, slack 150)
add P037 in 2030: breaks budget_2030 (needs 2,120, slack 50)
add P037 in 2031: breaks budget_2031 (needs 2,120, slack 130)
add P002 in 2027: breaks alt_G001 (slack 0), budget_2027 (needs 460, slack 140)
add P002 in 2028: breaks alt_G001 (slack 0), budget_2028 (needs 460, slack 150)

The 13 unfunded projects have 25 possible starts between them, and not one fits. Every budget row refuses some of them, and `budget_2030`, the year with $50k left, refuses 15 of the 25: it is the tightest rule in the plan although it does not bind. P004 needs $300k in 2028, where $150k is left; P002 is refused twice over, by its alternative row and by the money.

This is what a binding-constraints report on a MILP is for: a table with, per row, its slack, its price where the model has one, and what it refuses. The third column is what a planner means by "the 2030 budget is what's binding": not that it is used to the dollar, but that it is too full for any project left out.

The test has a limit worth saying in the report. It adds one project to the plan *as it stands*. The solver is free to do more: drop one project, move two others, and then fit the new one. Whether that is worth doing, and what it costs, is a question for a re-solve, which lesson 9.3.2 asks.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **A row binds when the plan leaves it no slack.** Slack is measured from the plan and the row, with no help from the solver, so it works on any model. On a MILP, the once, must, alt and after rows that bind mostly record what was chosen.

**A MILP has no prices, and binding means zero slack even when the price is zero.** MathOpt raises `ValueError` for MILP duals. In the LP relaxation, 11 GridCap rows bind at price 0; that is degeneracy, not "non-binding". Report the price in its own column.

**On a MILP, a row with slack can still be the row that blocks.** Whole projects cannot use the last few dollars. List, for each row, the single additions it refuses; on GridCap small no unfunded project fits, and the 2030 budget refuses 15 of 25 starts.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** the OR-Tools [MathOpt overview](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (models kept separate from solvers, and the dual solutions MathOpt can return); [MathOpt `result.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/result.py) (the docstrings of `dual_values` and `has_dual_feasible_solution`: dual solutions only for convex problems, and the `ValueError` when the best solution has none); [MathOpt `linear_constraints.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/linear_constraints.py) (a row's `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` and `terms()`, which `slack` reads); the [Gurobi reference for linear constraint attributes](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/current/reference/attributes/constraintlinear.html) (`Slack` is a property of the current solution, and `Pi` exists only for continuous models, the same split as MathOpt's); [Integer Programming, Chapter 9 of Applied Mathematical Programming (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-09.pdf) (section 9.1: capital budgeting as go/no-go variables against one resource row per period, the shape of GridCap's budget rows). The CIPT job this course prepares for lists binding constraints first among the outputs that explain a result.
Challenges

items: Lower the 2030 budget by $50k so that `budget_2030` binds, re-solve, and predict whether the plan changes. Then run it.
Which once rows would bind at price 0 in the LP if every project were a must-do? Think about what the budget rows would then have to do.
Extend `refusals` to try adding *two* unfunded projects at once. How many pairs are there on GridCap small, and why does the count make a re-solve the better tool?

blocks.text: Design Note: Read Binding From the Plan, Not From the Solver's Status Codes

An LP solver also reports a **basis status** for each row (`constraint_status`, lesson 2.3.3): a row `AT_UPPER_BOUND` is tight. It is tempting to build the report from those codes. They exist only for an LP solved by simplex, and a MILP has none. They also describe the solver's basis rather than the plan: `zero_price.py` asks for the status of the 11 rows that bind at price 0, and gets
basis status of the binding rows priced 0: {'BASIC': 11}

All 11 are tight, and the basis calls every one of them `BASIC`, the status lesson 2.3.3 met on a row with room (its slack in the basis): at a degenerate vertex a basic slack can sit at exactly zero. Slack computed from the plan and the row works on every model, every solver and every plan, including one a planner typed in by hand. Keep the solver's numbers as extra columns, never as the definition.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**slack_report.py.** Solves GridCap small and prints the binding rows by family, and the budget rows with their slack (*A Row Binds When the Plan Leaves It No Slack*). *Try:* Print the once rows that have slack. Predict which projects they belong to before you run it.

**zero_price.py.** Shows that the MILP has no dual values, then sorts the LP relaxation's rows by slack and price (*A MILP Has No Prices*). *Try:* Make P003 cost 400 instead of 140 in the program's copy of the portfolio. Predict whether `must_P003` keeps its zero price.

**refusals.py.** Tries every single addition to the base plan and counts the rows that refuse each (*On a MILP, a Row With Slack Can Still Be the Row That Blocks*). *Try:* Raise the 2030 budget by $300k. Predict how many of the 25 additions fit.
**binding.py** and **explain_model.py.** The report's two functions, and the named model with its `slack` and `plan_values`. They run nothing themselves.
